slides.notes:
Hi, we are Team Cosmic Cats from Amman. Our project is Analog Atlas.
In one sentence: it finds the Moon and Mars on Earth, using real, sourced data, not guesses. Values are measured where possible; where they are not, the app says 'not measured'.

items.text: NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE 2026 · AMMAN
ANALOG ATLAS
Find the Moon and Mars on Earth.
A 3D atlas of the places on Earth that behave like the Moon and Mars, built on real, sourced data.
Challenge: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
Team Cosmic Cats

Mohammad Fathi Awni Ahmad · Ameer Hamam
Abdalrhman Ali Samih Alhaj Hassan · Moath Abu Aisha
App screenshot · Earth: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble (NASA GIBS)

slides.notes:
To go to the Moon or Mars, NASA first tests everything on Earth, in places called analogs.
Look at these two photos: one is the Moon, one is Iceland. Hard to tell!
But looking alike is not enough. Which places really match a Moon base site or a Mars landing zone, in temperature, ground and rock? The data exists, but it is spread over many datasets.

items.text: 01 · THE PROBLEM
Before anyone flies, everything is tested on Earth.

Crews, rovers, suits and drills train in “analog” places on Earth.
But which places really behave like a Moon base site or a Mars landing zone?
The answer is spread over many NASA datasets, and analogs are often picked by how they look.
One is the Moon. One is Iceland.
THE MOON · Apollo 11, 1969
EARTH · Holuhraun, Iceland
Photos: NASA / Neil Armstrong, Apollo 11 (panorama assembly Yuri Krasilnikov) · NASA Johnson Space Center / Robert Markowitz. Public domain.

slides.notes:
Analog Atlas is a 3D globe of Earth, the Moon and Mars that runs in the browser.
You pick one of 13 targets, for example Jezero Crater on Mars or one of three permanent Moon base sites near the south pole, and the app ranks 19 Earth sites by how closely they match it.
You can fly to each place, stand there, and compare real photos side by side in Twin view.

items.text: 02 · OUR SOLUTION
Analog Atlas
A 3D globe of Earth, the Moon and Mars, in the browser.

Pick one of 13 targets: 3 Moon base sites, Moon ice, a Moon cave, Apollo sites, Mars landing sites and a Mars cave.
It ranks 19 Earth analog sites on 6 continents, with open, sourced data.
Fly down to any place in 3D and stand there.
Twin view: real photos of the Earth site and its target, side by side.
Twin view · Harrat al-Shaam (Jordan) and Jezero Crater (Mars)
The Moon’s south pole · Malapert Massif
App screenshots. Photos: Mohammad hajeer / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 (cropped) · NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/ASU · Moon: NASA LRO

slides.notes:
Each Earth site gets a score from four pillars: climate, terrain, geology and resources. The flat landing zone is shown next to it, but by default it does not change the score.
For the Moon base sites, climate also compares Sun height, how high the Sun gets in the sky, computed from latitude on both sides.
Climate, terrain and landing zone come from data: NASA POWER and MODIS on Earth, LRO on the Moon, NASA's orbiters and rovers on Mars, and elevation maps of all three worlds. Rock type and resources are sourced classifications: each one has a published source and an exact quote.
Where a value is a general figure and not a measurement at the site, the app labels it, and weak data gets a flag. If something was not measured, the app says 'not measured'. We never invent a number.
Satellites also show what the ground is made of: MODIS, Sentinel-2, ASTER and NASA's EMIT. The app shows it next to the score, but it never changes the score.

items.text: 03 · HOW WE SCORE
Four scored pillars, every value with its source.

items.title: Climate
items.body: Mean temperature, daily swing, coldest ground, rain and albedo. Moon base sites add Sun height.
items.source: NASA POWER 2001–2020 · MODIS · LRO Diviner · Mars Climate Sounder

items.title: Terrain
items.body: How steep the ground is in a 10 km box, on the same 500 m grid on all three worlds.
items.source: Copernicus DEM · LRO LOLA · MGS MOLA

items.title: Flat zone
items.body: Shown, not scored: the largest flat square with every slope under 10°, after NASA’s Artemis landing rule.

items.title: Geology
items.body: The main rock type: the same, related or different.

items.title: Resources
items.body: Water ice, caves for shelter, regolith to build with, salts and brines.
items.source: Every tag has a source and an exact quote

items.text: No guessing: a value that was not measured is shown as “not measured”, and weak data gets a ⚑ flag.
Also measured from orbit, shown but never scored: MODIS, Sentinel-2, ASTER and NASA EMIT show what the top of the ground is made of.
Photo: Harrat al-Shaam, Mohammad hajeer / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 (cropped, darkened)

slides.notes:
Here are some results, with the default screening settings.
For Jezero Crater, where Perseverance is driving, the best Earth twin is Harrat al-Shaam, the black basalt desert in north-east Jordan, at 66 percent. It also has lava caves: it is the best Jordan match for the cave targets, 71 percent for the Moon's Mare Tranquillitatis pit, where it is also the world number one, and 84 percent for the Arsia Mons skylight on Mars, one point behind Craters of the Moon in the USA. These two are our starred pairs, and the base plan is built on them.
For Gale Crater, Dalangtan playa in China comes first at 68 percent; for Phoenix, Tso Kar in India at 73. Harrat al-Shaam comes first for Apollo 11 at 67 percent, and second for Apollo 17.
For the three permanent Moon base sites near the south pole, the Dry Valleys of Antarctica lead for Malapert, Haughton Crater in Canada for Mons Mouton, and Jordan's Wadi Rum for the Shackleton connecting ridge, at 54 percent.
A score is not proof. It tells you where to test first.
Then we scored all of Jordan, 886 boxes of 10 kilometres, with the same method. One box 37 kilometres north-west of Wadi Rum has a median slope of 8.44 degrees; the Shackleton ridge has 8.56. That is a satellite result; nobody has checked it on the ground yet.

items.text: Screening score, default settings: 4 pillars. A match says where to test first, not proof. ⭐ = strongest Jordan match on each world (Mars: Craters of the Moon, USA, is #1 at 85 %, one point ahead). Apollo 17: Craters of the Moon 58 %. Base sites: Malapert, Mons Mouton, Shackleton ridge. Data flag ⚑: the climate cells of Tso Kar and the Dry Valleys sit over 400 m off the ground.
Discover Jordan

We scored all of Jordan the same way: 886 boxes of 10 km. One box 37 km north-west of Wadi Rum has a median slope of 8.44°; the Shackleton connecting ridge on the Moon has 8.56°. Found by satellite data, not field-checked yet.

slides.notes:
Our method has four steps: target profile, Earth screening, field calibration and an explained score. Steps one and two are the app. For step three we designed a low-cost rover with the rocker-bogie suspension used on Mars since Sojourner, carrying a spectrometer, a soil probe, LiDAR and climate sensors on an ESP32. Its field readings will calibrate the satellite data, and later train a model that ranks unvisited Moon and Mars areas. It is a concept; it is not built yet.
Our honest status: every match today comes from satellite data and published sources. Nobody has checked the Discover boxes on the ground yet. Our next step is a field visit in Jordan, to Harrat al-Shaam and the box near Wadi Rum, to measure temperature, slope and rock, and compare them with the data.
Already in the app, as a concept for future work: Base plan draws a 3D base at each starred pair, with a hydroponic greenhouse, where potato, soybean and lettuce are the best low-cost set, and a communications room: a message to Mars takes 3 to 22 minutes, so families send video messages.
After that: more countries, and sharing the atlas with mission teams and students.

items.text: 05 · FROM DATA TO THE FIELD
Next: check the ground in Jordan.

Every match today comes from satellites and published sources.
The next step is a field visit: measure temperature, slope and rock at Harrat al-Shaam and at the box near Wadi Rum, and compare with the data.
Next steps

Field method: a low-cost rocker-bogie rover (ESP32, spectrometer, soil probe, LiDAR) measures the top candidates on site and calibrates the satellite data. Concept, not built yet.
Base plan (a concept, in the app): a 3D test base at each ⭐ pair, with a hydroponic greenhouse and a communications room.
Bring Discover to more countries; share it with mission teams and students.
